User is interested in the history of photography and asked about straight photography, Paul Strand, Frances Benjamin Johnston, and Charles Dudley Arnold (conversation 2023-05-20). #photography

Straight photography is an early-20th-century style (flourished 1920s-30s) aiming at direct, objective, unmanipulated images with no artistic effects or darkroom trickery. #straight-photography #photography
Alfred Stieglitz, photographer and critic, coined/popularized the term "straight photography" and championed photography as an art form in its own right. #straight-photography #photography

Straight photography grew partly in reaction to Pictorialism's artistic manipulation while sharing the documentary tradition's social focus; key photographers include Edward Weston, Paul Strand, and Ansel Adams. #straight-photography #photography

Paul Strand (1890-1976) was an American modernist photographer, a pioneer of straight photography and an influence on documentary photography; largely self-taught, he joined Stieglitz's Photo-Secession in 1915. #paul-strand #photography #straight-photography
Paul Strand's notable work includes a series on the people and landscapes of Mexico begun in 1932; he believed photography could be a tool for social change. #paul-strand #photography

Frances Benjamin Johnston (1864-1952) was an American photographer, one of the first women to build a professional photography career in the US; she opened her own Washington, D.C. studio in 1894. #frances-benjamin-johnston #photography

Frances Benjamin Johnston was known for elegant portraits of politicians, celebrities, and socialites (e.g., Theodore Roosevelt, Mark Twain, Susan B. Anthony) and for pioneering architectural photography documenting America's historic buildings. #frances-benjamin-johnston #photography

Charles Dudley Arnold (1865-1946) was an American photographer discussed for pioneering aerial photography, first from balloons in the 1890s and then from airplanes in the early 1900s, working with aviators such as Orville Wright. #charles-dudley-arnold #photography #aerial-photography

Charles Dudley Arnold also experimented with nighttime photography, using electric lights, gas lamps, torches, flash powder, and magnesium wire to capture dramatic, high-contrast urban night scenes. #charles-dudley-arnold #photography

User is designing/teaching a 15-week university course titled "Public Policy Analysis" (#PublicPolicyAnalysisCourse). Course description covers the concept and characteristics of public policy, models of public policy, the public policy analysis process (policy problems, policy alternatives, policy enforcement, policy implementation, policy assessment), strengths and limitations of analytical techniques, and examples of public policy research in Thailand and abroad.

#PublicPolicyAnalysisCourse CLO 1: Analyze the concept and characteristics of public policy (high-level Bloom's: understanding/evaluating), demonstrated via critical reading, written reflection on key readings, case studies, and policy issues — assessed in Weeks 1-5.

#PublicPolicyAnalysisCourse CLO 2: Evaluate the process of public policy analysis (Bloom's: analyzing/creating), demonstrated by designing and implementing policy analysis exercises such as cost-benefit analysis, multi-criteria decision-making, and advocacy coalition mapping, presented in class discussions and group projects — Weeks 6-14.

#PublicPolicyAnalysisCourse CLO 3: Evaluate strengths and limitations of analytical techniques in public policy analysis (Bloom's: analyzing/evaluating), demonstrated through critical analysis of policy research papers and developing the student's own policy analysis techniques — Weeks 6-14.

#PublicPolicyAnalysisCourse CLO 4: Synthesize and apply knowledge of public policy analysis to real-world policy issues (Bloom's: synthesizing/evaluating), demonstrated by independent research culminating in a final research paper incorporating policy research from Thailand and abroad — Weeks 10-15.

#PublicPolicyAnalysisCourse week-by-week topic flow (Weeks 1-11): 1 concept of public policy analysis; 2 policy cycle and policy subsystems; 3 policy implementation; 4 program evaluation techniques; 5 policy paradox framework; 6 role of bureaucracy in policy making; 7 bureaucratic accountability mechanisms; 8 cost-benefit analysis; 9 multi-criteria decision-making; 10 public value and stakeholder participation; 11 policy discourse analysis.

#PublicPolicyAnalysisCourse readings W12: Bardach & Patashnik (2016) A Practical Guide for Policy Analysis: The Eightfold Path (5th ed.), CQ Press; Howlett, Ramesh & Perl (2009) Studying Public Policy: Policy Cycles and Policy Subsystems (3rd ed.), Oxford UP.

#PublicPolicyAnalysisCourse readings W13: Fischer (2003) Reframing Public Policy: Discursive Politics and Deliberative Practices, Oxford UP; Hajer (1995) The Politics of Environmental Discourse: Ecological Modernization and the Policy Process, Oxford UP.

#PublicPolicyAnalysisCourse readings W14: Haas (1992) "Introduction: Epistemic Communities and International Policy Coordination," International Organization 46(1), 1-35; Jenkins-Smith, Nohrstedt, Weible & Sabatier (2014) "The Advocacy Coalition Framework" in Theories of the Policy Process (pp. 183-224), Westview Press.

#PublicPolicyAnalysisCourse readings W15: Grindle & Thomas (1989) Public Choices and Policy Change: The Political Economy of Reform in Developing Countries, Johns Hopkins UP; Andrews (2018) The Limits of Institutional Reform in Development: Changing Rules for Realistic Solutions, Cambridge UP.

#PublicPolicyAnalysisCourse assessments W1-W8: W1 class discussion on concept/significance of policy analysis; W2 written reflection on policy cycle and subsystems; W3 case study analysis of a policy's implementation; W4 group presentation on program evaluation techniques; W5 critical analysis using the policy paradox framework; W6 essay on bureaucracy's role in policy making; W7 written critique of a bureaucratic accountability mechanism; W8 cost-benefit analysis exercise.

#PublicPolicyAnalysisCourse assessments W9-W15: W9 group project on multi-criteria decision-making; W10 research paper on public value and stakeholder participation; W11 written policy discourse analysis; W12 policy memo using the eightfold path; W13 deliberation exercise on an environmental policy issue; W14 advocacy coalition mapping; W15 comparative analysis of institutional reform initiatives across countries.

#taj-mahal #user-interests The user was curious about the Taj Mahal in a conversation on 2023-05-30: they hadn't known it was built in memory of Shah Jahan's wife Mumtaz Mahal, found that "so romantic," and asked follow-ups about build time, marble transport, and the intricate carvings.

#taj-mahal The Taj Mahal was built by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Construction began in 1632 and the main structure took about 22 years; work on gardens and outbuildings continued until 1653. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site and a major tourism draw for India.

#taj-mahal Construction facts: roughly 20,000 artisans and laborers; cost estimated around 32 million rupees at the time (over a billion USD today); white marble quarried at Makrana, ~200 miles from Agra, carried by elephants to the Yamuna riverbank then by boat to the site.

#taj-mahal Decoration techniques: pietra dura inlay with semi-precious stones (lapis lazuli, agate, turquoise, jasper; roughly 28 stone types), Quranic calligraphy in stylized Arabic, and 3D relief marble carving done with chisels and hammers. A double dome helped distribute weight and keep the structure stable.
